Chapter 2: The Lost Tradition of Independent Thinking
You know, at the heart of every faith, there are these sparks of brilliance—moments when fresh ideas aren’t just welcomed, but celebrated. Times when open debate is encouraged, and searching for truth feels like a sacred mission.
For centuries, Islam was no different. Imagine a world where scholars didn’t just memorize ancient texts—they dove deep to really understand them. They argued, disagreed, and sometimes even admitted they’d changed their minds. This spirit of independent reasoning, called ijtihad, once breathed life into Islamic civilization.
But somewhere along the way, things started to shift. The doors to ijtihad—those doors of independent thought—began to close, one after another. Why? Well, it wasn’t just one reason. Political upheaval, fear of chaos, the urge to stay united when facing outside threats... all of these played a part.
Soon, the idea took hold that only a select few—people with the right credentials, the right lineage, maybe even the right connections—were truly qualified to interpret the faith. For everyone else? The message was clear: follow, don’t question.
And this shift had real consequences. Picture a family, sitting together. A father tries to explain why certain rules must be followed. His son, bright and curious, asks simple but powerful questions—like why women can’t lead prayers, or why non-Muslims are sometimes viewed with suspicion. The father, a bit uncomfortable, just repeats what he’s heard from the local imam: “These are the rules. It’s not for us to question.” The boy can sense his dad’s uncertainty, but also his fear. Because questioning? That can get you labeled a troublemaker—or worse.
In another town, a group of friends gathers after a sermon. One is a university student, and she wonders aloud if those verses about violence in the Qur’an are meant to be taken literally. The others shift uneasily, glancing at the door. They know what asking these kinds of questions can bring. Sometimes, it just feels safer to stay silent.
Most of us don’t even notice how this culture of silence seeps into daily life. It shapes how children are taught, how leaders speak, even how families talk to each other. Obedience becomes the most important thing, and anyone who dares to think for themselves is seen as a threat.
But here’s the thing—the tradition of ijtihad isn’t gone. Not completely. In quiet corners, away from the spotlight, some people still practice it. Picture a young woman, frustrated by all the contradictions she sees in her community. She picks up the Qur’an and starts reading for herself. She checks out different translations, compares interpretations, and asks the questions others are afraid to voice. Slowly, she discovers a faith that’s richer, more complex, and a whole lot more compassionate than what she was taught.
So, what’s the real danger? It isn’t in asking questions. It’s in refusing to ask them. When people stop thinking for themselves, they become easy targets for anyone who wants to use religion as a tool for control. They lose the ability to tell the difference between genuine faith and empty ritual, between justice and oppression.
The path to reform? It starts with reclaiming ijtihad—not just as something intellectual, but as a way of living. It means encouraging everyone to engage with their faith honestly, to wrestle with tough questions, and to realize that doubt isn’t the enemy of belief—it’s actually its companion.
Only then can Islam, once again, become a force for justice, compassion, and true human dignity.
